ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the ethics committee at Aalborg University, Denmark.

Participants completed immediate and delayed recall tasks, including two tasks assessing context-supported memory, and reported their general environmental preferences and preferences for the environments they experienced.
All participants completed each experimental condition, with exposure order counterbalanced across participants.
Following the encoding and Immediate Recall procedures across all four environments, participants completed a series of additional memory tasks.

Following a 30-minute break which was used to fill out the environmental preference questionnaire, participants completed Delayed Recall task, recalling objects from all four conditions irrespective of their original environmental context.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Environmental preferences vary between individuals, yet little is known about how these preferences relate to memory for information encountered in different environments.
We investigated this relationship in 60 participants using four virtual environments varying in environmental type (urban vs. natural) and spatial regularity (rhythmic vs. irregular).

Participants completed immediate and delayed recall tasks, including two tasks assessing context-supported memory, and reported their general environmental preferences and preferences for the environments they experienced.
General preferences for nature and spatial structure were not associated with memory performance.
However, contextsupported recall was higher for objects encountered in environments that participants subsequently identified as preferred.

These findings highlight the relevance of individual evaluations of specific environments for understanding memory in everyday settings, suggesting that the cognitive implications of environmental design may depend not only on environmental characteristics but also on how individuals experience and evaluate them.

Research on environment and cognition examines how characteristics of the physical environment relate to cognitive processes and behavior (Berman et al., 2019; Bratman et al., 2015; Djebbara et al., 2025; Fich et al., 2014; Hussein et al., 2026).

Environmental responses vary with prior experience and individual characteristics (Coutrot et al., 2022; Kuliga et al., 2019; Newcombe et al., 2022), while the experience and evaluation of natural environments also differ between individuals (Koivisto et al., 2022; Meidenbauer et al., 2019; Tost et al., 2019; Twedt et al., 2019; Wilkie & Delicato, 2026).

Understanding relationships between environments and cognition may, therefore, require consideration not only of environmental characteristics, but also of individual differences.
Environmental preferences may reflect evaluations of multiple environmental characteristics rather than responses to a single objectively defined feature.

Research has demonstrated that preferences vary with characteristics of environmental configuration (Coburn et al., 2020; Gregorians et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2018; Weinberger et al., 2021). Individuals may also evaluate specific environments differently, even when they share a general preference for the same environmental category.

General environmental preferences and preferences for specific experienced environments may, therefore, represent related but distinct levels of evaluation, with the latter reflecting responses to the configuration and experience of a setting.

This distinction aligns with calls for more specific characterization of environmental exposures and experiences beyond broad environmental classifications (Huynh, Hussein, Fich, et al., 2026a; Kühn et al., 2023; Mascherek et al., 2026; Sander et al., 2024; Zähme et al., 2026).

>Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Methods</head>

text.text: The present study examined associations between environmental preferences and episodic memory performance differing in environmental type (natural vs. urban) and spatial organization (rhythmic vs. irregular).
The study, thereby, employed a 2 × 2 within-subject design in which participants experienced four environments.
We considered environmental preference at two levels of specificity.

First, we examined whether general preference for natural environments was associated with memory performance across natural and urban environments, and preference for spatial structure versus variation was associated with memory performance across rhythmic and irregular environments.
We then examined whether memory performance differed according to participants' preferences for the specific environments they had experienced.

Episodic memory was assessed through Immediate and Delayed Free Recall and two context-supported Guided Recall tasks, allowing us to investigate whether preference-memory associations varied across retrieval conditions.

Particular attention was given to the Guided Recall tasks, which involved retrieving object-environment associations in complementary directions, to examine whether environmental preference was associated with memory when retrieval involved the original environmental context.
All participants completed each experimental condition, with exposure order counterbalanced across participants.
The experiment was conducted in virtual reality (VR), allowing participants to physically move and explore the environments.
All the environments were matched in overall spatial dimensions, while their visual composition and spatial organization varied according to the experimental manipulations (Figure 1).
text.formatted: All the environments were matched in overall spatial dimensions, while their visual composition and spatial organization varied according to the experimental manipulations (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Rhythmic environments were characterized by regular, symmetrical arrangements of environmental elements, whereas irregular environments contained greater variation in element orientation and placement.
In the urban-irregular environment, this variation also extended to the orientation of surrounding buildings.
The terms rhythmic and irregular, thus, describe the experimentally manipulated spatial organization rather than participants' subjective evaluations of the environments.
Experimental objects occupied identical spatial locations across all four environments, ensuring that object position was held constant across conditions.
At the beginning of each condition, participants freely explored the environment for one minute before completing an object-search task.
Using a handheld VR controller, participants searched for eight objects distributed throughout the environment and interacted with each by pointing at and selecting it with the controller (Figure 2).
text.formatted: Using a handheld VR controller, participants searched for eight objects distributed throughout the environment and interacted with each by pointing at and selecting it with the controller (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: The objects within each environment belonged to different semantic categories to minimize semantic associations between them.
After locating all eight objects, participants remained in the same environment and completed an Immediate Recall task, recalling as many of the encountered objects as possible.
This procedure was repeated across all four environments, with oneminute breaks between conditions.
Following the encoding and Immediate Recall procedures across all four environments, participants completed a series of additional memory tasks.
First, in a neutral virtual environment, they completed a Free Recall task, recalling as many objects as possible across all conditions, irrespective of their original environmental context.
Participants then completed two context-supported recall tasks.
In Guided Recall 1, they returned to each experimental environment and recalled the objects previously encountered there.
In Guided Recall 2, previously encountered objects were presented individually, and participants identified the environment in which each object had appeared.
One-minute breaks separated the memory tasks.

Following a 30-minute break which was used to fill out the environmental preference questionnaire, participants completed Delayed Recall task, recalling objects from all four conditions irrespective of their original environmental context.
General environmental preference captured participants' preference for natural vs. urban environments.

Preference for spatial organization assessed the extent to which participants preferred orderly and structured environments vs. environments characterized by variation and spontaneity, reflecting the regularity dimension manipulated in the experiment.
Participants were also asked to select which of the four experimental environments they preferred overall and, separately, which they would prefer for concentration and learning.

For these measures, observations from the selected environment were coded as preferred and observations from the remaining three environments as non-preferred, allowing memory performance in the subsequently preferred environment to be compared with performance in the other environments.
Overall environmental preference constituted the primary preference measure.
Participants additionally reported the perceived complexity of their childhood environment to capture previous environmental experience.
Perceived safety was assessed but, due to limited variability, was included only in supplementary analyses (Figure 3).

Participant measures captured general preferences, preferences for the specific environments experienced, and environmental background.
Preferredenvironment status indicated whether memory performance corresponded to the environment subsequently selected as preferred.

Memory outcomes included free recall, in which objects were recalled without explicit support from the environmental context, and context-supported recall, in which retrieval required objectenvironment associations.

The statistical analyses examined whether memory performance was associated with environmental preference while accounting for environmental condition, presentation order, and repeated observations within participants.
Linear mixed-effects models were used as the primary analytical approach, with participant included as a random effect.
The main outcome was a context-supported recall index, constructed to capture memory performance when retrieval explicitly depended on the relation between objects and their environmental context.

Guided Recall 1 required participants to recall objects within their original environment, whereas Guided Recall 2 required participants to identify the original environment associated with each object.
Although the tasks differed in retrieval direction, both therefore depended on object-environment associations.

To provide a common measure of contextsupported recall, Guided Recall 1 and Guided Recall 2 were z-scored across observations and averaged, with higher values indicating stronger context-supported recall.

The main predictor of interest was preferred-environment status, indicating whether an observation came from the environment that the participant subsequently identified as their preferred environment.
Preferred-environment status was coded separately for each observation by comparing the current virtual environment with each participant's selected preferred environment.
Each participant therefore contributed one preferred-environment observation and three non-preferred-environment observations.

To determine whether the association with preferred-environment status was independent of participants' broader preference for natural versus urban environments, Nature Preference was added to a second model:
This model tested whether preferred-environment status remained associated with context-supported recall after accounting for general Nature Preference.
The contribution of preferred-environment status was further evaluated by comparing this model with a reduced model that omitted preferredenvironment status.
Model comparison was conducted using a likelihood-ratio test, alongside AIC, BIC, and marginal and conditional R² as indices of model fit.
Sixty participants (f = 33) were recruited from the local university community through social media and university recruitment portals.
Participants had a mean age of 24.15 years (SD = 1.96, range = 21-30 years).
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and reported no known psychological diagnoses.
Participants received financial compensation for their participation.
All experimental sessions were conducted in the afternoon to maintain consistency in the timing of testing and environmental light exposure.
The study received ethical approval from the university's ethical review board and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 2025).
Participants received written information about the study via email before participation, including information concerning the study procedures, potential risks, benefits, and data handling.
This information was reiterated at the beginning of the experimental session, at which point participants were given an additional opportunity to ask questions before providing written consent.
Participation was voluntary, and participants were informed of their right to withdraw at anytime.
Data were treated confidentially and stored securely in accordance with the approved data-management procedures.
>Results
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Results</head>

text.text: Initial mixed-effects analyses examined memory performance across environmental conditions and recall tasks.
Immediate Recall 1 and Immediate Recall 2 showed no statistically significant main effects of environmental type or structural regularity, nor interactions between these factors (all p > .05).
text.formatted: Immediate Recall 1 and Immediate Recall 2 showed no statistically significant main effects of environmental type or structural regularity, nor interactions between these factors (all p > .05).

text.text: In contrast, Guided Recall 1 showed a significant Environment × Regularity interaction (β = 1.25, 95% CI [0.41, 2.09], p = .004), with the highest recall observed in the nature-irregular condition.
Guided Recall 2 showed a positive but non-significant effect of irregularity (β = 0.55, 95% CI [-0.02, 1.12], p = .056), but no significant interaction (β = 0.22, p = .594).

Although condition-specific contrasts indicated higher Delayed Recall in the nature-irregular condition than in the other environments, these differences were no longer evident after accounting for earlier recall performance.

Together, these analyses indicated that memory performance varied across environmental conditions and retrieval tasks, providing a basis for examining whether individual environmental preferences were associated with memory beyond the experimentally manipulated environmental characteristics (Figure 4).

>Discussion
text.formatted: <head n="4." >Discussion</head>

text.text: The present findings suggest that context-supported recall was higher in environments that participants subsequently identified as preferred, whereas general preferences for nature and spatial structure were not associated with memory performance.
This association remained evident after accounting for the experimentally manipulated environmental characteristics and presentation order.
The findings suggest that evaluations of specific environmental experiences may be more informative about memory performance.
The present findings extend previous evidence linking environmental evaluation and memory by distinguishing between what is remembered and the conditions under which remembering takes place.

Whereas Babo-Rebelo et al. (2022) examined aesthetic experience in relation to spatial memory, and Momenzadeh et al. (2026) investigated preferences for architectural interiors in relation to incidental recognition memory, the present study examined memory for objects encountered within different environments.
Importantly, the association with preference was not evident across all retrieval tasks.
Momenzadeh et al. ( 2026) observed an association with delayed, but not immediate, recognition, whereas the present study found the clearest association during context-supported recall.
text.formatted: Momenzadeh et al. ( <ref type="formula">2026</ref>) observed an association with delayed, but not immediate, recognition, whereas the present study found the clearest association during context-supported recall.

text.text: Although the tasks differ, it suggests that the relationship between environmental evaluation and memory may depend on the information being remembered and the conditions under which retrieval takes place.
In the present experiment, this was particularly relevant when participants returned to previously encountered environments or identified the environment in which an object had been experienced.

Rather than indicating a general memory advantage associated with preferred environments, it suggests that environmental evaluation may be particularly relevant when remembering involves drawing on relationships between encountered objects and their environmental contexts.
The distinction between broad and specific environmental preferences further qualifies these findings.
Although most participants selected one of the natural environments as their preferred setting, general nature preference did not moderate memory responses to natural vs. urban conditions.
General preferences for nature may reflect influences extending beyond the immediate characteristics of an environment.

Cross-cultural differences in landscape preferences have been documented by Hägerhäll et al. (2018), while Jensen and Olsen (2019) examined the relationship between childhood nature experiences and environmental preferences in adulthood.
text.formatted: Cross-cultural differences in landscape preferences have been documented by <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Hägerhäll et al. (2018)</ref>, while <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Jensen and Olsen (2019)</ref> examined the relationship between childhood nature experiences and environmental preferences in adulthood.

text.text: Similarly, van den Berg (2021) has argued that preferences for natural over built environments, and their restorative effects, may be influenced by learned associations and culturally transmitted expectations.

Although the present findings cannot distinguish between these explanations, they illustrate that a general preference for nature does not necessarily correspond to episodic memory performance within natural environments.
Likewise, preference for spatial structure vs. variation did not account for memory responses to rhythmic vs. irregular environments.

Thus, a strong group-level preference for natural environments coexisted with individual variation in the specific environment preferred, while broader preference measures provided little information about memory performance.

This distinction is consistent with evidence that individual differences in preference extend to particular perceptual characteristics (Cotter et al., 2017). Morton et al. (2017), furthermore, found that cognitive and motivational responses to natural environments depended on whether those environments corresponded with a salient social identity, with benefits emerging when the environment was identity-consistent and reversing when it was not.

(2017)</ref>, furthermore, found that cognitive and motivational responses to natural environments depended on whether those environments corresponded with a salient social identity, with benefits emerging when the environment was identity-consistent and reversing when it was not.

text.text: Although identity congruence differs from environmental preference, it illustrates that responses to an environmental category may depend on the relationship between the individual and the setting.

Knowing which of the four experienced environments a participant preferred was, therefore, more informative about context-supported recall than knowing whether they generally preferred nature or a particular form of spatial organization.
This does not imply that broad environmental preferences are irrelevant.

Rather, preferences measured at different levels of specificity may capture different aspects of environmental evaluation (Huynh, Hussein, Behzadi, et al., 2026b , 2026a), in which a general preference for nature reflects an evaluation of a broad environmental category, whereas preference for a specific environment reflects an evaluation of a particular configuration of characteristics as encountered and experienced by an individual.
text.formatted: Rather, preferences measured at different levels of specificity may capture different aspects of environmental evaluation <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Huynh, Hussein, Behzadi, et al., 2026b</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2026a)</ref>, in which a general preference for nature reflects an evaluation of a broad environmental category, whereas preference for a specific environment reflects an evaluation of a particular configuration of characteristics as encountered and experienced by an individual.

text.text: These levels of preference should, therefore, not necessarily be expected to correspond to the same outcomes.
Importantly, however, environment-specific preference was assessed only after participants had completed the memory tasks.
Consequently, the direction of the observed association cannot be established.
One possibility is that participants remembered objects more successfully because they experienced a specific environment more positively.
Conversely, they may have evaluated an environment more positively because objects encountered within it were easier to remember or because remembering within that environment was more successful.
These possibilities are not mutually exclusive.
Preferences need not constitute fixed evaluations that precede an experience but may themselves develop through experiences available in memory (Weber & Johnson, 2006).
text.formatted: Preferences need not constitute fixed evaluations that precede an experience but may themselves develop through experiences available in memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">(Weber & Johnson, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Processing fluency may also contribute to positive evaluations, such that experiences that are easier to process are subsequently evaluated more favorably (Reber et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Processing fluency may also contribute to positive evaluations, such that experiences that are easier to process are subsequently evaluated more favorably <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Reber et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: The present findings, therefore, do not demonstrate that environmental preference caused better memory.
Instead, they identify an association between subsequent evaluations of specific environments and memory for information encountered within them.
From this perspective, environment-specific preference may be understood as an overall evaluation emerging from the interaction between an individual and a specific setting.

Such an evaluation may reflect multiple aspects of the experience, including familiarity, visual engagement, affective responses, perceived distinctiveness, and ease of interaction (Gregorians et al., 2022; Reber et al., 2004; Vartanian et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Such an evaluation may reflect multiple aspects of the experience, including familiarity, visual engagement, affective responses, perceived distinctiveness, and ease of interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Gregorians et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Reber et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">Vartanian et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, positive environmental evaluations do not necessarily correspond to more favorable physiological or cognitive responses.

In an exploratory study, Schuller et al. (2026) found that softer, more homely environments were associated with greater physiological arousal, while participants' subjective accounts suggested potential tensions between comfort and the ability to focus.

(2026)</ref> found that softer, more homely environments were associated with greater physiological arousal, while participants' subjective accounts suggested potential tensions between comfort and the ability to focus.

text.text: These evaluations may also be shaped by previous environmental experiences, with familiarity influencing responses to different environments (Cipriani et al., 2026), and subjective and physiological responses varying with how environments are experienced (Koivisto & Grassini, 2023 , 2024).
text.formatted: These evaluations may also be shaped by previous environmental experiences, with familiarity influencing responses to different environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Cipriani et al., 2026)</ref>, and subjective and physiological responses varying with how environments are experienced <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Koivisto & Grassini, 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Environment-specific preference may, therefore, be informative because it reflects aspects of the relationship between an individual and an environment that are not adequately captured by broad environmental categories or isolated environmental characteristics.
The association between environment-specific preference and context-supported recall may also relate to how individuals encounter, explore, and engage with their surroundings.

Rather than preference directly benefiting memory, both environmental evaluation and subsequent remembering may be related to aspects of the experience, including attention, affective responses, and engagement.

Research has demonstrated that motivational significance can influence memory performance, with effects observed in relation to reward, curiosity, and choice (Adcock et al., 2006; Gruber et al., 2014; Knowlton & Castel, 2022; Murty et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Research has demonstrated that motivational significance can influence memory performance, with effects observed in relation to reward, curiosity, and choice <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adcock et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Gruber et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Knowlton & Castel, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Murty et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Although preference for an environment cannot be equated with these forms of motivational value, this literature provides a basis for considering whether the subjective significance of an environment may be related to how individuals engage with information encountered within it.
In this sense, preference may reflect aspects of the individual's ongoing interaction with the environment.
In the present experiment, participants freely navigated the environments while encountering objects, allowing for potential differences in how they explored and attended to their surroundings.

Previous research has demonstrated associations between patterns of visual exploration and subsequent memory performance (Celli et al., 2025; Kafkas & Montaldi, 2011), with Alderman et al. (2026) urther showing that the organization of gaze, including refixations and spatial distribution, was informative about scene memory precision.

text.text: Although these findings concern different experimental contexts, they suggest that attention and exploration may be relevant to understanding the observed association between environmental preference and memory.
The pattern of memory performance provides a further consideration.
Although differences were evident in context-supported recall, differences in delayed recall were no longer evident after accounting for earlier memory performance.
This suggests that differential retention alone is unlikely to account for the observed pattern.

Instead, the association may relate to processes occurring during initial encounters with objects or subsequent retrieval opportunities, both of which can influence later remembering (Pastötter et al., 2011; Uncapher & Rugg, 2005).

text.text: However, the present study cannot distinguish between these possibilities, nor did it measure gaze behavior or attentional allocation.
The literature on attention and exploration, therefore, provides a direction for future investigation rather than an explanation established by the present findings.
However, the present study cannot distinguish differences arising during initial learning from those arising during subsequent retrieval, nor did it measure gaze behavior or attentional allocation.

These studies, therefore, provide a possible direction for future investigation, rather than an explanation directly supported by the present data, particularly regarding how visual exploration, attention, and object-environment associations may contribute to the relationship between environmental preference and memory.
A further, exploratory finding concerned participants' previous environmental experiences.
Childhood environmental complexity was associated with one Guided Recall measure, although this relationship was not consistent across the other Guided Recall task or Delayed Recall.
A related association was observed in a separate study of architectural rhythm and episodic memory (Huynh, Fich, & Djebbara, 2026).

text.text: Although these findings should be interpreted cautiously, they raise the possibility that previous experience with different forms of spatial organization may be relevant to how individuals engage with and remember information in subsequent environments.

Research has linked childhood exposure to street-network complexity with adult navigation performance, particularly in environments resembling those experienced during upbringing (Coutrot et al., 2022), while other studies have similarly associated previous spatial experience with navigation abilities (Yavuz, He, et al., 2024; Yavuz, Manley, et al., 2024).

text.text: Although these findings concern navigation rather than episodic recall, they suggest that previous environmental experience may be relevant to investigating individual differences in environment-memory relationships.
The association between environment-specific preference and memory was most evident when retrieval involved the environmental context in which objects had been encountered.
Whereas preference was not associated with Immediate Recall, it was associated with both Guided Recall tasks, suggesting that the relationship was not uniform across memory outcomes.

This distinction is consistent with research demonstrating that the contribution of environmental context to remembering depends on retrieval conditions. Barak et al. (2013) found that reinstating environmental context influenced free and guided recall but not recognition, while Cox et al. (2023) demonstrated that reinstating elements of the original context can facilitate episodic retrieval.

text.text: In the present study, the association with preference was particularly evident when participants either returned to the environment in which objects had been encountered or were asked to identify that environment from an object.

This suggests that the relationship between environmental evaluation and memory may be particularly relevant when remembering involves drawing on relationships between objects and their surrounding environments.

One possible explanation concerns how objects and environmental cues become associated through experience. Hayes et al. (2007) demonstrated that changes in scene context can impair subsequent object recognition, illustrating how remembering objects may depend on the contexts in which they were originally encountered.

(2007)</ref> demonstrated that changes in scene context can impair subsequent object recognition, illustrating how remembering objects may depend on the contexts in which they were originally encountered.

text.text: Masís-Obando et al. ( 2026), additionally, examined how differences in the neural reliability of spatial contexts related to later memory.
text.formatted: Masís-Obando et al. ( <ref type="formula">2026</ref>), additionally, examined how differences in the neural reliability of spatial contexts related to later memory.

text.text: Their findings suggest that spatial contexts may differ in how they support subsequent remembering, with individual differences in neural responses also playing a role.

Related research has further shown that architectural aesthetics and spatial complexity are associated with activity in brain regions involved in memory and environmental experience (Gregorians et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Related research has further shown that architectural aesthetics and spatial complexity are associated with activity in brain regions involved in memory and environmental experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Gregorians et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In the present experiment, participants encountered objects while exploring distinct environments, and the association between preference and Guided Recall may, therefore, be related to differences in how objects and environmental cues were experienced together or subsequently drawn upon during retrieval.

However, the present study did not independently measure the development or strength of object-environment associations, and the findings cannot establish whether such differences account for the observed relationship.
A related possibility concerns the distinctiveness of environmental contexts, as distinctive contextual information can facilitate recognition when reinstated during retrieval (Park et al., 2006).
text.formatted: A related possibility concerns the distinctiveness of environmental contexts, as distinctive contextual information can facilitate recognition when reinstated during retrieval <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Park et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Although the environments in the present experiment differed in spatial organization, including rhythmic and irregular arrangements, these differences cannot be equated with perceived contextual distinctiveness, which was not independently assessed.

The contribution of environmental context may also depend on retrieval goals. Elward and Rugg (2015) demonstrated that retrieval goals influence which aspects of a previous experience are recovered, while Gardette and Bastin (2026) showed that information treated as a focal item may instead function as context depending on what is being retrieved.
text.formatted: The contribution of environmental context may also depend on retrieval goals. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Elward and Rugg (2015)</ref> demonstrated that retrieval goals influence which aspects of a previous experience are recovered, while <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Gardette and Bastin (2026)</ref> showed that information treated as a focal item may instead function as context depending on what is being retrieved.

text.text: This is particularly relevant to the present experiment, in which Guided Recall 1 required participants to recall objects while revisiting their original environment, whereas Guided Recall 2 required them to identify the original environment associated with a presented object.
Unlike these tasks, Immediate Free Recall did not explicitly require participants to draw on environmental context.

The association with preference across both Guided Recall tasks is, therefore, consistent with the possibility that environment-specific evaluations relate to remembering when object-environment relationships are relevant to retrieval, although the underlying contribution of contextual distinctiveness remains untested.

Taken together, these findings suggest that the relationship between environmental preference and memory may be better understood in relation to the circumstances under which environmental context contributes to remembering, rather than as a general advantage of preferred environments.
Contextual associations, perceived distinctiveness, and retrieval demands offer complementary perspectives on why environmental contexts may contribute differently to recall.
However, the present experiment cannot determine which of these processes, if any, accounts for the association with subsequently reported preference.
What the findings demonstrate is that this association was particularly apparent when remembering involved the environments in which objects had been encountered.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings.
Most importantly, environmental preference was assessed after completion of the memory tasks rather than measured independently beforehand.
Consequently, the observed association between preferred-environment status and context-supported recall does not establish that preference improved memory.

Participants may have engaged differently with environments they subsequently preferred, but their preference judgments may also have been influenced by their experiences during the experiment, including their perceived success in remembering objects, even though no feedback on memory performance was provided.

Although the analyses accounted for repeated observations within participants, presentation order, and the experimentally manipulated environmental conditions, they cannot resolve the direction of this relationship.
Furthermore, each participant identified only one preferred environment among four alternatives, resulting in one preferred and three non-preferred observations per participant.
This comparison captures the distinction between the most preferred environment and the remaining alternatives, rather than a continuous relationship between degrees of preference and memory.
It, therefore, remains unknown whether memory performance varies systematically across different levels of environmental preference.
The processes underlying the association also remain unresolved.

Although the study examined memory while participants actively explored virtual environments, it did not independently assess attention, visual exploration, affective responses, motivational engagement, or the strength of object-environment associations.

Consequently, the potential contributions of these processes cannot be distinguished, and the mechanisms discussed in the preceding sections should be understood as possibilities rather than explanations demonstrated by the experiment.
Future studies incorporating these elements could help clarify how preference and memory become related during environmental encounters.
The specificity and measurement of environmental preference also warrant consideration.

General preference for nature and preference for spatial structure vs. variation were not consistently associated with memory, whereas preference for the specific environment was associated with context-supported recall.
However, these measures differed in their content, scale, and operationalization.
Environmentspecific preference was expressed as a choice among four experienced settings, whereas the broader measures assessed more general environmental preferences.
Their different associations with memory, therefore, cannot be attributed to the specificity of preference alone.

Furthermore, perceived suitability for concentration and learning was not significantly associated with either Guided Recall measure, despite the association observed for overall environmental preference.

Research suggests that preferences for learning environments may reflect perceived suitability for particular activities (Beckers et al., 2016), while positive environmental evaluations do not necessarily correspond to improved cognitive performance (van den Bogerd et al., 2020 (van den Bogerd et al., , 2021)).

text.text: Nevertheless, the absence of a significant association should not be interpreted as evidence that perceived suitability is unrelated to memory.
Moreover, preference for a particular environment was assessed at a single time point, providing no information about how evaluations might develop through repeated encounters.

Research on favorite places suggests that environmental preference, personal experiences, memory, and place attachment can become intertwined over time (Korpela et al., 2001; Ratcliffe & Korpela, 2016; Subiza-Pérez et al., 2021).

text.text: Although familiar and personally meaningful places differ substantially from the novel virtual environments examined here, this literature highlights the importance of examining how environmental evaluations and memories may develop together rather than treating preference as a stable characteristic preceding experience.

The present study suggests that the relationship between environmental preference and episodic memory depends on both the specificity of the preference and the conditions under which memory is assessed.
General preference for nature and preference for spatial structure vs. variation showed little association with memory performance.
In contrast, context-supported recall was higher for objects encountered within the environment that participants subsequently identified as their preferred one.

This association was evident after accounting for the experimentally manipulated environmental characteristics, suggesting that evaluations of specific environments may capture aspects of individual experience not adequately described by broad environmental categories alone.
These findings highlight the importance of considering environmental characteristics alongside individual evaluations when investigating how environments relate to cognition.
Although natural environments were generally preferred, this did not translate into a corresponding association between general nature preference and memory.

Moreover, the relationship between environment-specific preference and memory was not uniform across retrieval tasks, suggesting that environmental evaluations may be particularly relevant when remembering involves drawing on the context in which information was encountered.
Importantly, because preference was assessed after the memory tasks, the direction of this relationship remains unresolved.
The findings, therefore, do not establish that preferred environments improve memory, nor do they identify a particular environmental configuration as universally beneficial.

For the study and design of learning and working environments, the findings suggest that environmental characteristics and individual experience should be considered together rather than assuming that the same spatial configurations will support cognition equally across people and tasks.

This does not imply designing environments solely around stated preferences, but instead points toward examining how different environmental characteristics are encountered and evaluated in relation to cognitive activities.
